title: Estimating depth from a flat street image
caption: Final published article, Figure 3. The source’s depth-output example illustrates the attempt to distinguish foreground and background before estimating pairwise spacing. The color values are model output, not calibrated physical distance or a measure of a person’s identity. The complete source figure is reproduced without altering its contents.
alt: Original false-color depth map of a street scene, with people in the foreground and background.
credit: Caliskan et al., Scientific Reports (2025), Figure 3; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

title: Relative spacing across visible category pairs
caption: Final published article, Figure 5. Estimated contrasts in normalized distance from the cross-group reference, with the full specification’s controls. NRF/NRM mean non-religious female/male; RF/RM mean religious female/male as visually classified. Negative values indicate smaller relative distances, not fewer meters or proven political hostility. The complete source figure is reproduced without altering its contents.
alt: Coefficient plot showing especially negative normalized-distance estimates for pairs classified as religious women.
credit: Caliskan et al., Scientific Reports (2025), Figure 5; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

title: Agreement in ranking, compression in scale
caption: July 2024 SSRN/USC manuscript, Figure 3. The horizontal axis is the human-coded RILE benchmark and the vertical axis the model-derived score. The dashed identity line represents perfect agreement; flatter fitted model lines show compressed ideological differences. The original figure calls the benchmark “ground truth,” though the text discusses ambiguities in human coding.
alt: Scatterplot of five models’ RILE estimates against human manifesto scores, with fitted lines flatter than the identity line.
credit: Caliskan et al., Using Generative AI to Calculate Party Positions, July 2024 manuscript, Figure 3.

title: False claims combine several themes
caption: Final published article, Figure 3 (printed page 199). Diagonal cells count claims in each topic; other cells count topics appearing together. Colors use a logarithmic scale and blank cells indicate zero co-occurrences. These are coded items in a fact-check corpus, not population exposure or belief.
alt: Heatmap of COVID-19 falsehood topics and their co-occurrences, with counts printed in each cell.
credit: Caliskan and Kilicaslan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 3; published online 2022.

title: Comparing content across press-freedom groups
caption: Final published article, Figure 13 (printed page 215), rotated for reading. Each row compares misinformation-content similarity within or between press-freedom categories. The within-group comparison for countries with a “very serious situation” has higher similarity and substantial variation. This is an association in selected fact-check records, not a causal estimate of censorship.
alt: Horizontal boxplots comparing misinformation similarity across pairs of press-freedom categories.
credit: Caliskan and Kilicaslan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 13; published online 2022.

title: Daily changes in pandemic-related attention
caption: Final published article, Figure 8 (printed page 36). Stacked daily values show the paper’s computational topic-awareness measure for January–April 2020. Vertical lines mark first cases and policy dates. The figure shows changes in conversation and event timing; it does not measure the causal effect of a policy.
alt: Daily stacked bars of Ohio Twitter topic-awareness estimates, showing a large March increase in illness-related attention.
credit: Cantay Caliskan, Journal of Computational Social Science, Figure 8; published online 2021.

title: The policy network extends beyond ministers
caption: Final published article, Figure 1: Iceland Minister-to-Friend Network. Red nodes are ministers and gray nodes are accounts they follow. Shared gray nodes connect different ministers’ circles; a follow is a proxy for a relationship, not direct evidence of policy influence.
alt: Iceland’s minister-to-friend network, with red minister nodes and gray followed accounts in connected clusters.

title: Community structure and renewable-energy outcomes
caption: Final published article, Figure 8. Panels (a) and (b) show model-based marginal relationships for the last-ten-year and last-five-year outcome averages. Higher cross-community linkage and lower modularity are associated with higher renewable-energy outcomes; shaded uncertainty bands are part of the source figure. These are observational country comparisons, not causal effects.
alt: Six original marginal-effect plots, comparing cross-community links, modularity and centrality skewness with renewable-energy outcomes.
